pillar_reactions.evidence: Agreed without questions — 'No, all makes sense.' The pillar was partly customised to him, with the rep referencing his specific history: 'because your back went out in the past and also with the left elbow issue, Trevor is going to make a specific mobility program for you as well.' Worth noting that a substantial portion of this block was spent on battle maces, a piece of equipment the prospect had never heard of and would not use, which the manager criticised in the review of this call: 'I don't want to hear you getting into long rants about an app or about kettlebells and why you should do a battle mace.'

Accepted it while noting it described what he already does, which is agreement that also quietly deflates the pillar's value: 'Yeah, it's kind of like where I'm at right now, so that works, yeah.' The rep had opened the block by acknowledging 'you're already doing quite okay on that' and the only concrete change proposed was removing sugar from his coffee — a change the prospect had already made himself and reported on earlier in the call.

Engaged only on logistics: 'No. What time is the workout on Thursdays?' — the sole question asked across the whole pillar. No enthusiasm and no objection. He had already told the rep that accountability was not his gap, describing an established habit — 'I just get up in morning and I go... that's just who I am' — and identified his actual needs as kettlebell form and phase-two programming, so the pillar the offer leans hardest on addressed a problem he did not have.

anchors.raw: You know, no idea. think I saw on your site that you do, like, $1.99 a month for some kind of, like… So, like, I saw that and I was, you know, like, yeah, that's not crazy. So maybe that's why I had that number in my head.
anchors.competitor: Primal Instinct's own publicly advertised $199 per month community product
anchors.note: The most important anchor in the batch because it is self-inflicted and independently corroborated. The prospect arrived with $199 a month in his head from the company's own website, then heard $6,000, a roughly forty-fold gap. The rep acknowledged the product exists and explained why he had withheld it: 'the reason I didn't offer you that was because when you mentioned you want the guidance, you want to make sure your forms correctly... I don't think that's, like, the best thing to do.' The same mechanism appears in the coaching one-to-one an hour later, where the rep reports a different prospect lost the same day for the same reason and the manager advises not to worry about it.

anchors.raw: I'm doing well enough with my own cutting. The program is well enough, probably at least all of this, at least to get me to the next 30, 60 days, you know, so that those are the two things.
anchors.competitor: His own free, currently working calisthenics and deficit programme
anchors.note: Unusually strong because it is demonstrably succeeding: 20 lb lost in three months, steps from 4,000 to 11,000, a tracked strength progression, and a self-described identity shift, all without paying anyone. He named the two conditions that would change his mind — money becoming a non-issue, or exhausting his own knowledge — and estimated the second at 30 to 60 days away. With no consequence frame run, deferring was the rational choice and the offer gave him no reason it was not.

anchors.raw: trainer was like five, six years ago, you know, and then after that, you know, COVID, two kids, you know, so it was just like completely back burner.
anchors.competitor: A personal trainer he used five or six years ago
anchors.note: No price attached and never used as a comparison, so a weak anchor — recorded because it is the only paid coaching in his frame of reference and it ended without lasting effect, which cuts against the value case rather than for it.

unmet_demand.want: Anything written describing what six months and $6,000 actually includes — 'if you have a white paper or a PDF of what's included for the six months, maybe even a schedule or something'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No such document exists. The rep answered plainly: 'Actually, we don't really have it written out, to be honest. Basically, how it's gone, I've become completely trained, of course, on what we specifically have, and it's all in here.' A buyer deferring a five-figure Canadian-dollar decision was left with nothing to review or reason about between calls.

unmet_demand.want: A monthly payment option without a premium attached
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Instalments were available but priced at an extra $200 a month, described as processing fees, taking the total from $6,000 to $7,200. The prospect had already said he would consider monthly and was explicitly weighing roughly $1,000 a month against his runway; the surcharge moved it further out of reach rather than closer.

unmet_demand.want: Expert guidance on how long to stay in a deficit, the hormonal cost of extended cutting, and how to transition into a lean bulk — his stated reason for being on the call
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Answered off the cuff by the salesperson rather than deferred to the coach. Asked directly whether cutting beyond six months affects hormones, the rep gave an opinion: 'with cutting sometimes you want to go a little bit longer even though that might outbalance your hormones for a short time.' The programme presumably covers this properly through Trevor, but the prospect's specific technical question was handled by someone not positioned to answer it.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that progressive kettlebell loading will not re-trigger a back that took a year of physiotherapy to settle, or fail an elbow he can already feel going
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Acknowledged and folded into a promised custom mobility programme, but never assessed. No question about whether physiotherapy had discharged him, no clinician contact suggested, and no follow-up when he named injury as the single thing that could stop him.
